**Monday, February 29, 1960**

A date that most calendars simply skip. In sixty-six years you have had sixteen true birthdays — the rest borrowed from February 28 or March 1. The rarity of the day is part of its character: you arrived on a date the world only occasionally admits exists, in a year that was itself a threshold between one era and the next.

---

**The Agadir earthquake — exact date**

On the night of February 29, 1960, an earthquake struck Agadir, Morocco while most of the city slept. The tremor was moderate by seismic standards but devastating in effect: shallow, fast, and arriving at 11:40 PM when people were in their homes and their beds. In fifteen seconds, between 12,000 and 15,000 people died — roughly a third of the city's entire population. Agadir was rebuilt on a different site, on a new plan, as if the old city had simply been erased. The day that became your birthday was, for an entire Moroccan city, an extinction event. It is one of the stranger things about arriving on a specific date in history: you share it with catastrophes and celebrations in equal measure, none of which had anything to do with you.

---

**Between Sputnik and Mercury — the space race at its pivot**

You were born in the narrow window between the shock of Sputnik and the first human spaceflight. The Soviet Union had launched Sputnik in October 1957, and the sound of its radio beep — broadcast on American television — had produced something close to national panic. By February 1960, NASA was deep in the preparation of Project Mercury; Alan Shepard would become the first American in space in May 1961, fifteen months after your birth. The Soviets were further ahead than anyone in the West fully understood: Yuri Gagarin would orbit the Earth in April 1961. You were born during the brief period when space travel was imminent but had not yet happened — when the race was being run in laboratories and on launchpads, and no one yet knew who would arrive first.

---

**The decade turning — Kennedy and the sense of threshold**

February 1960 was two months into a new decade, and the new decade felt like something. Eisenhower was in his final year, visibly aging, presiding over a country that had grown prosperous and was beginning to feel restless with its prosperity. John F. Kennedy had just announced his presidential campaign, and what he represented — youth, speed, a break from the generals and elder statesmen who had governed since the war — was already legible before a single primary had been held. The television debates that autumn, in which Kennedy appeared composed and Nixonappeared sweating and pale, had not yet happened, but television itself was already reshaping everything it touched. You were born in the last weeks of one political era and the first stirrings of the next.

---

**The Year of Africa arriving — the world remaking its map**

The decolonization wave you were born into was not abstract. Seventeen African nations would gain independence in the calendar year of your birth. Many of them were unprepared — not through any failure of their people, but because colonial administrations had deliberately withheld education, governance experience, and infrastructure from their populations for generations. Congo, which became independent in June 1960, had fewer than thirty university graduates in the entire country at the moment of independence. The Year of Africa was a genuine liberation and, in many places simultaneously, an invitation to chaos that outside powers — Belgian, French, American, Soviet — were quick to exploit. The world this person was born into was shedding empire faster than it could build what came next.

---

**±30-day worldwide event: The Sharpeville massacre — March 21, 1960, twenty-one days after your birth**

Twenty-one days after you were born, South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black protesters at Sharpeville, outside Johannesburg. The demonstrators had gathered to protest the pass laws — the apartheid system's requirement that Black South Africans carry identity documents at all times or face arrest. Police fired into the crowd as it was dispersing. Sixty-nine people were killed; most were shot in the back. More than 180 were wounded. The photographs circled the globe. International condemnation was swift and intense; South Africa was censured at the United Nations. The African National Congress was banned. Nelson Mandela and the ANC's leadership concluded that nonviolent resistance was no longer viable and turned toward armed struggle. Sharpeville did not end apartheid — that would take another thirty-four years — but it established the terms of the conflict that would consume South Africa for the rest of the century. It happened three weeks after you arrived.

---

**The lifetime that followed**

Sixteen birthdays. Sixty-six years. You were nine when Armstrong walked on the Moon — the culmination of the space race that was just beginning when you were born. Twenty-three when HIV/AIDS was named and no one yet knew where it had come from or where it would go. Twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall fell. Forty-one on September 11, 2001. Sixty-three when the pandemic began. Your most recent actual birthday — February 29, 2024 — was your sixteenth. The next is February 29, 2028.

In the sixty-six years between the Agadir earthquake and today: the polio vaccine in widespread use, the contraceptive pill, the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, gene sequencing, the Mars rovers, and now artificial intelligence capable of generating conversation. The world of that Monday night in 1960 — its space race still undecided, its African nations just arriving at independence, its South Africa still a generation away from ending apartheid — is another world entirely.

---

**What kind of world did you enter?**

You were born on a day that exists only by mathematical necessity, into a year that was genuinely a turning point. The sixties had just begun and had not yet become the sixties. Space was about to be entered by human beings for the first time. Africa was remaking its own map. A new American president was about to be chosen by television. In South Africa, three weeks after your birth, sixty-nine people would die for carrying the wrong paperwork.

The world of February 29, 1960 was one in motion — large structures breaking, large possibilities opening. The child born on that rare Monday entered a river already moving fast. It has not slowed since.
